t: Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 265-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 10 of 49 Kratom is considered a drug of concern by the US Drug Enforcement Administration, and the FDA has issued an Import Alert identifying kratom as a New Dietary Ingredient (NDI) for which a reasonable expectation of safety has not been established. Kratom leaves produce over 25 alkaloid compounds. The most prominent psychoactive components are: (1) mitragynine (MTG); and (2) 7- hydroxymitragynine (7HMG). Both MTG and 7HMG are agonists at the mu-opioid receptor. 7HMG is considered nine times more active than MTG. Clinical effects of mitragynine are in part related to the mu-opioid receptor activity, additionally mitragynine has been reported to bind to other receptors including adrenergic, serotonin and dopamine receptors. Kratom has polypharmacologic activity including stimulant, opioid, and sedative type effects. Both the effect and toxicity of kratom are dose related. Documented symptoms include but are not limited to respiratory depression, cardiac arrythmias, prolonged QT, seizures, liver impairment, and psychosis. Regular consumption of kratom is associated with tolerance and dependency, requiring ingestion of higher doses to achieve similar effect. Kratom related deaths involve clinical findings consistent with opioid toxicity, intractable seizures, and cardiorespiratory arrest. Often, when an individual dies from elevated opiate levels, the cause is properly attributed to a chronic dependency leading to escalated doses that exceed therapeutic levels. The same process occurs with kratom, with the important exception that those selling the kratom frequently do not provide warnings or safe instructions for use and dosing. This includes drug interactions or interactions with underlying health conditions. Kratom’s adverse effects include severe dependence negatively affecting physical well-being and opioid-like withdrawal symptoms requiring medical intervention after addiction to kratom. A case report of an individual using kratom for chronic pain documented a pattern of daily kratom consumption in which tolerance development for analgesic effects was overcome by an increase in daily consumption. Ultimately, the high kratom dosing provided less relief and started to induce fatigue and drowsiness and rather prevented the patient from work and an active lifestyle. The patient ultimately required professional help for kratom withdrawal. Kratom also acts as a stimulant. Stimulants like kratom have the potential to cause enlargement of the heart. An enlarged heart is a heart that is electrically susceptible to arrythmias. The stimulant effects of kratom increase the likelihood of electrical instability and sudden cardiac death. The stimulant effect of kratom has

On February 6, 2023, Harmony Moller (DOB: 02/18/1986) was discovered by her mother, Kathleen Moller, unresponsive in her bedroom. Nearby, Defendants’ kratom products were discovered. Paramedics were called. EMS records note Harmony was in asystole, and resuscitation was attempted via compressions and ventilation. However, Ms. Moller remained without any pulse, any cardiac activity, or spontaneous respirations or movements, and she was therefore pronounced dead. The investigation by law enforcement and the medical examiner did not find signs of foul play or suicide. The foregoing context supports the conclusion that Harmony Moller died from an adverse cardiorespiratory event caused by kratom. My review of the medical and death records stated above included findings of pulmonary edema and congestion, chronic passive congestion of the liver, and mild nephrosclerosis, high origin of left coronary artery, and cardiomegaly. Cardiomegaly is a finding that Harmony’s heart was enlarged. As noted above, enlargement of the heart may be caused by repetitive use of stimulants, like kratom. These conditions may have been co-morbidities for Harmony Moller but were not the primary cause of death. The primary cause of death was a cardiorespiratory event caused by kratom. The toxicology results from NMS Labs directly support kratom’s causative role in Harmony’s death. The blood concentration of Mitragynine was 150 ng/ml, a level sufficient to cause adverse events. A blood concentration of 7- hydroxymitragynine at 0.8 ng/ml was also present. The toxicology results also returned a positive result for caffeine, a finding expected in individual who ingested caffeinated products such as coffee. Naloxone was also positive. The naloxone was administered by first aid responders according to EMS records. Delta-9 THC and Delta-9 Carboxy THC were also present at low levels. These concentrations are not consistent with a toxic or fatal ingestion. Diphenhydramine was present at a concentration of 64 ng/ml. Said concentration is not consistent with a fatal or toxic dose. Promethazine was present at a concentration of 18 ng/ml. Said concentration is not consistent with a fatal or toxic dose. The concentrations of diphenhydramine and promethazine are consistent with therapeutic dosing, and therefore unlikely to be a cause or contributor of Harmony Moller’s death. The toxicology results confirm that the cause of death was directly related to kratom. I conclude from the historical context, the medical examiner’s report, the heart pathology report, and the toxicology results that kratom caused the adverse cardiorespiratory death of Harmony Moller. This conclusion is being made with a reasonable degree of medical certainty.

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF DEFENDANTS’ MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT Defendants LP Ind., LLC (“LP”); CAG Holdings, LLC (“CAG”); RMH Holdings, Inc. (“RMH”); Martian Sales, Inc. (“Martion Sales”); Johnson Foods, LLC (“Johnson Foods”); JOpen, LLC (“JOpen”); Nuza, LLC (“Nuza”); Calibre Manufacturing, LLC (“Calibre”); FMK Group, Inc. (“FMK”); PNW Holdings, LLC; CC US Holdings, LLC (“PNW”); Peyton Palaio; Mark Jennings; David Gabbay; and Mark Reilly (collectively “Defendants”) who respectfully submit this memorandum in support of their summary judgment. I. INTRODUCTION This matter concerns Plaintiff Kathleen Moller’s “products liability claims under Louisiana’s Products Liability Act, La. R.S. 9:2800.51, et seq., asserting that the kratom product consumed by Harmony [her daughter] was unreasonably dangerous due to a failure to warn and a design defect.” Order and Reasons, ECF No. 184, at 2; see also Third Amended Complaint (“TAC”), ECF No. 100. O.P.M.S. Silver kratom is the sole product at issue in this lawsuit. The O.P.M.S. Silver allegedly consumed by Harmony Moller is a pure kratom leaf powder that was sold lawfully in Louisiana at the time she allegedly purchased it from unknown third-party

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 2 of 27 retailers. Defendants are not retailers and did not sell any product to Plaintiff. For each Defendant, summary judgment is warranted for multiple, independent reasons. First, there is no evidence supporting a conclusion that any of Defendants LP, CAG, RMH, Johnson Foods, FMK, PNW, or CC US is a manufacturer of O.P.M.S. Silver, as required under the Louisiana’s Products Liability Act (“LPLA”) to support a products liability claim. These defendants have no involvement with or control over O.P.M.S. Silver kratom products, so a products liability claim necessarily fails. In addition, Plaintiff has no evidence to support individual liability against Peyton Palaio, Mark Jennings, David Gabbay, or Mark Reilly (the “Individual Defendants”). These defendants had no involvement with the O.P.M.S. Silver product at issue outside of their formal managerial roles with the corporate defendants. Plaintiff’s theory that the corporate defendants serve as these individuals’ alter egos fails under the applicable legal standards. Plaintiff’s core theory of products liability—that O.P.M.S. Silver was simply too dangerous to be sold—likewise fails as a matter of law. Plaintiff’s daughter Harmony is alleged to have consumed O.P.M.S. Silver in February 2023 when kratom was sold legally in Louisiana— just as it continues to be sold legally both federally and most other states. Plaintiff’s argument that kratom should have been illegal in 2023 ignores the simple fact that kratom was legally sold in Louisiana when Harmony purchased it. It certainly does not give rise to a product liability design defect claim. Louisiana product liability law requires a plaintiff claiming a design defect—as a threshold matter—to provide specific, product-level evidence of the existence of alternative design for kratom that was capable of preventing the claimant’s damage. Plaintiff offers none. Plaintiff’s case also fails due to an utter lack of proof of causation. All parties agree that a sudden cardiac event caused Harmony’s death. It is undisputed that Ms. Moller had a coronary 2

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 3 of 27 anomaly described as an “abnormally high left coronary ostia takeoff.” The coroner performed a limited postmortem toxicology test that confirmed the presence of at least two prescription drugs (promethazine and diphenhydramine, neither of which prescribed to Harmony) that are scientifically proven to cause cardiac arrhythmias through QT prolongation. The postmortem level of mitragynine, an alkaloid in kratom, was at an exceedingly low level—one that scientific literature has shown is safe and well-tolerated. Plaintiff’s entire case rests on the speculative leap that this low level of mitragynine, and not the combination of a serious heart defect and other potent drugs, was the cause of her daughter’s death. This speculation is compounded by the fact there is no direct evidence Ms. Moller even consumed Defendants’ O.P.M.S. Silver product before her death. Plaintiff asks this Court to ignore these fatal evidentiary gaps and proceed to trial on conjecture alone. Finally, Plaintiff’s failure to warn claim fails because a manufacturer cannot be required to warn of a risk that is scientifically unknown or unforeseeable. In February 2023, there was no scientific or medical data to suggest that a low, well-tolerated level of mitragynine could cause a fatal cardiac event. The claims also fail because any additional warning would have been futile. The O.P.M.S. Silver packaging contained a robust warning that explicitly instructed the user to consult a physician before use—a warning Harmony undisputedly ignored. Plaintiff cannot prove causation, cannot satisfy the statutory elements of her LPLA claims, and has sued parties with no legal connection to her alleged harm, and no genuine issues of material fact remain for trial. Defendants are entitled to judgment as a matter of law. II. SUMMARY OF STATEMENT OF MATERIAL FACTS A. Harmony Moller. 3

SOF ¶ 94. Harmony’s postmortem level of 150 ng/mL was less than a tenth of the lowest level found in that study. SOF ¶ 94. III. ARGUMENT A. Summary judgment standard. Summary judgment is appropriate where there is no genuine disputed issue as to any material fact, and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56; Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 322, 106 S. Ct. 2548, 2552, 91 L. Ed. 2d 265 (1986); Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 247, 106 S. Ct. 2505, 2509-10, 91 L. Ed. 2d 202 (1986). A party moving for summary judgment must inform the Court of the basis for the motion and identify those portions of the pleadings, depositions, answers to interrogatories and admissions on file, together with affidavits, if any, that show that there is no such genuine issue of material fact. Celotex Corp., 477 U.S. at 322. If the moving party carries its burden of proof under Rule 56, the opposing party must direct the Court’s attention to specific evidence in the record which demonstrates that the non-moving party can satisfy a reasonable jury that it is entitled to a verdict in its favor. Anderson, 477 U.S. at 248. This burden is not satisfied by some metaphysical doubt as to alleged material facts, by unsworn and unsubstantiated assertions, by conclusory allegations, or by a mere scintilla of evidence. Little v. Liquid Air Corp., 37 F.3d 1069, 1075 (5th Cir. 1994). Rather, Rule 56 mandates that summary judgment be entered against a party who fails to make a 8

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 9 of 27 showing sufficient to establish the existence of an element essential to that party’s case and on which that party will bear the burden of proof at trial. Celotex Corp., 477 U.S. at 323. B. Plaintiffs’ claims against numerous defendants fail as a threshold matter. 1. Numerous corporate Defendants are not manufacturers of O.P.M.S. Silver as a matter of law. Plaintiff brings each of her claims against Defendants under the LPLA. ECF No. 100 at ¶¶ 61–64. The first element of a claim under the LPLA is that “the defendant is a manufacturer of the product.” Jefferson v. Lead Indus. Ass’n, Inc., 106 F.3d 1245, 1251 (5th Cir. 1997). “Plaintiff’s obligation to identify the manufacturer of the allegedly defective product is inherent in the LPLA’s requirement that plaintiff prove proximate causation.” Id. at 1252. Plaintiff alleges that her daughter, Harmony Moller, consumed O.P.M.S. Silver kratom and that this product contributed to her death. ECF No. 100 ¶¶ 30, 33. Plaintiff, however, cannot raise a genuine issue of material fact that any of Defendants LP, CAG, RMH, Johnson Foods, FMK, PNW, or CC US is a manufacturer of O.P.M.S. Silver kratom. Plaintiff thus cannot meet her burden to prove any of those Defendant proximately caused her injury. La. R.S. 9:2800.53(1) defines “Manufacturer” to mean “a person or entity who is in the business of manufacturing a product for placement into trade or commerce” wherein “‘Manufacturing a product’ means producing, making, fabricating, constructing, designing, remanufacturing, reconditioning or refurbishing a product.” The statute provides that “Manufacturer” also means “[a] person or entity who labels a product as his own or who otherwise holds himself out to be the manufacturer of the product.” La. R.S. 9:2800.54(B)(1)(a). It is undisputed that Defendant Calibre is a kratom manufacturer that puts kratom powder into capsules and sends bulk kratom product to Defendant JOpen in Texas. SOF ¶¶ 49, 50. It is undisputed that Defendant JOpen then oversees packaging and distributes products, including the 9

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 10 of 27 O.P.M.S. Silver product at issue, using O.P.M.S. trademarks owned by Defendant Martian Sales. SOF ¶ 21. In contrast, Defendants LP, CAG, RMH, CC US, PNW, FMK, or Johnson Foods are not involved with the producing, making, fabricating, constructing, designing, remanufacturing, reconditioning or refurbishing of O.P.M.S. Silver products. SOF ¶¶ 31, 34, 37, 39, 41, 43, 46. There is therefore no triable issue of fact as to whether any of Defendants LP, CAG, RMH, Johnson Foods, FMK, PNW, or CC US qualify as a Manufacturer under the LPLA. The Court should therefore grant summary judgment in favor of those Defendants as to all claims brought against them. 2. Plaintiff cannot seek liability against the Individual Defendants. Plaintiff brings each of her claims against Defendant Peyton Palaio as a member of Defendants Nuza, Calibre, LP, RMH, PNW, and CC US. ECF No. 100, ¶¶ 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 18, 20, 21. Plaintiff brings each of her claims against Defendant Mark Jennings as “an individual who is closely associated and involved with” business operations of O.P.M.S. branded kratom products. Id., ¶ 22. Similarly, Plaintiff brings her claims against each of Eyal David Gabbay and Mark Reilly as “an individual who is closely associated and directly involved with the kratom business operations of the O.P.M.S. brand.” Id., ¶¶ 23–24. A bedrock principle of corporate law is that an individual who incorporates a business is shielded from personal liability for the corporation’s obligations. See Riggins v. Dixie Shoring Co., Inc., 590 So. 2d 1164, 1167–68 (La. 1991). To hold an individual liable for the actions of a corporate entity, a plaintiff must pierce the corporate veil, a remedy reserved for “exceptional circumstances.” Id. at 1168. Plaintiff’s theory for holding the Individual Defendants liable rests entirely on her conclusory allegation that they are the “alter egos” of the corporate entities. ECF No. 100, ¶ 25. After full discovery, Plaintiff has failed to produce any evidence that would justify such a drastic remedy. Nothing in the record shows that Messrs. Palaio, Jennings, Gabbay, or 10

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 11 of 27 Reilly acted outside their capacities as managers, members, or officers of their respective companies. In that motion, Plaintiff argued that “[t]he standard for veil piercing for jurisdictional purposes is lower.” ECF No. 132-1 at 19. However, Plaintiff’s statement of facts in support of that motion failed to provide the Court with any evidence that could possibly justify piercing the corporate veil with respect to any of the Individual Defendants for jurisdictional purposes—let alone for liability. See generally ECF No. 132-2; see also ECF No. 143 at 16–17. Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 12 of 27 a. Plaintiff cannot show JOpen’s corporate veil should be pierced. “Louisiana courts have not explicitly ruled on the appropriate choice of law for veil piercing theories. However, the Fifth Circuit has predicted that Louisiana courts would look to the law of the state in which the defendant corporation was incorporated.” Louisiana Newpack Shrimp, Inc. v. Ocean Feast of China, Ltd., 19-129948-WBV-KWR, 2021 WL 516631, at *7 (E.D. La. Feb. 11, 2021). It is undisputed that JOpen is a Texas company. ECF No. 132-2, ¶¶ 8–9. Under Texas law, “to pierce the corporate veil and impose liability under an alter-ego theory, the plaintiff must demonstrate (1) that the entity on which it seeks to impose liability is the alter ego of the debtor, and (2) that the corporate fiction was used for an illegitimate purpose, that is, to perpetrate an actual fraud on the plaintiff for the defendant’s direct personal benefit.” U.S. KingKing v. Precision Energy Servs., 555 S.W.3d 200, 212 (Tex. App.—Houston [1st Dist.] 2018, no pet.); see also Metroplex Mailing Servs v. RR Donnelley & Sons Co., 410 S.W.3d 889, 896-97 (Tex. App.— Dallas 2013, no pet.) (“Evidence that a company was used as an alter ego does not, by itself create an issue regarding whether it was used to commit an actual fraud on the plaintiff for the defendant's personal benefit.”). Plaintiff has failed to provide any facts supporting a claim that any of the Individual Defendants is the alter ego of JOpen, nor has Plaintiff alleged that any of the Individual Defendants used “the corporate fiction . . . to perpetrate an actual fraud on the plaintiff for the defendant’s direct personal benefit” as required under Texas law. Accordingly, there is no basis for piercing JOpen’s corporate veil to find any Individual Defendant personally liable for the acts of JOpen. b. Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 13 of 27 Calibre, FMK, PNW, and CC US are all Wyoming companies. See ECF No. 132-2 at ¶¶ 6–7, 10– 27. Wyoming veil-piercing law thus applies to determine whether any of the Individual Defendants can be held personally liable for any of their actions. Louisiana Newpack Shrimp, 2021 WL 516631, *7 Under Wyoming law, “[b]efore a corporation’s acts and obligations can be legally recognized as those of a particular person, and vice versa, it must be made to appear that the corporation is not only influenced and governed by that person, but that there is such a unity of interest and ownership that the individuality, or separateness, of such person and corporation has ceased, and that the facts are such that an adherence to the fiction of the separate existence of the corporation would, under the particular circumstances, sanction a fraud or promote injustice.” Ridgerunner, LLC v. Meisinger, 2013 WY 31, ¶ 14, 297 P.3d 110, 115 (Wyo. 2013). “The veil of a limited liability company may be pierced under exceptional circumstances when: (1) the limited liability company is not only owned, influenced and governed by its members, but the required separateness has ceased to exist due to misuse of the limited liability company; and (2) the facts are such that an adherence to the fiction of its separate existence would, under the particular circumstances, lead to injustice, fundamental unfairness, or inequity.” Greenhunter Energy v. Western Ecosystems, 337 P. 3d 454, 461 (Wyo. 2014). “In determining whether both prongs of this test have been met, courts can usually apply several factors. . . The first is whether there has been fraud. . . . Second, inadequate capitalization, if there is evidence of it, may be considered. . . . however . . . undercapitalization alone will not suffice to pierce the veil. . . . A third factor to consider is the degree to which the business and finances of the company and the member are intermingled.” Id., at 463–64. As to the fraud factor, “[t]he elements of a claim for relief for fraud are a false representation made by the defendant which is relied upon by the 13

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 14 of 27 plaintiff to his damage, the asserted false representation must be made to induce action, and the plaintiff must reasonably believe the representation to be true. A plaintiff who alleges fraud must do so clearly and distinctly, and fraud will not be imputed to any party when the facts and circumstances out of which it is alleged to arise are consistent with honesty and purity of intention. Fraud must be established by clear, unequivocal and convincing evidence, and will never be presumed.” Id. at 470. Plaintiff has failed to produce any evidence that could establish that any of the veil-piercing factors are met as to any of the Wyoming LLCs or corporations. The requirement of a “false representation made by the defendant which is relied upon by the plaintiff to his damage” is alone dispositive. Plaintiff has no evidence of such a false representation, or any reliance on one, so none of the Wyoming LLCs’ or corporation’s veil’s may be pierced to impose personal liability on any of the Individual Defendants. Accordingly, the Court should summarily dismiss the claims against the Individual Defendants because Plaintiff cannot carry her burden to show any genuine issue of material fact that could permit corporate veil-piercing. 3. Courts reject efforts to impute manufacturer status to related parties absent extraordinary circumstances. Finally, Plaintiffs invoke alter ego not to remedy fraud in a creditor setting, but to convert individuals and affiliated entities into statutory “manufacturers.” The LPLA is explicit: only a “manufacturer” may be held liable for product defects. La. R.S. § 9:2800.52. The statute carefully limits liability to the entities that actually design, manufacture, assemble, or otherwise place the product into the stream of commerce. Plaintiff attempts to use veil-piercing as an end-run around the LPLA’s manufacturer limitation. Courts do not permit that. Alter ego is an extraordinary equitable remedy, and particularly disfavored when used to 14

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 15 of 27 expand statutory strict products liability rather than to prevent asset shielding after judgment. The Fifth Circuit has warned against expanding manufacturer liability through alter ego. In Rodriguez v. Riddell Sports, Inc., 242 F.3d 567, 573 (5th Cir. 2001), the Fifth Circuit reversed a jury verdict that had treated multiple related entities and individuals as manufacturers in a products liability case under an alter ego theory. Although Rodriguez applied Texas law, its reasoning is directly applicable here because both Texas and Louisiana treat veil piercing as a “radical” and “extraordinary” remedy. Id. at 374 (“Generally, a court will not disregard the corporate fiction and hold a corporation liable for the obligations of its subsidiary except where it appears the corporate entity of the subsidiary is being used as a sham to perpetrate a fraud, to avoid liability, to avoid the effect of a statute, or in other exceptional circumstances.”). Louisiana law is the same: “‘[p]iercing the corporate veil is considered a radical remedy,’” and “the principle that the corporation is a separate entity should be disregarded only in exceptional circumstances.” Patz v. Sureway Supermarket, No. CV 17-3465, 2018 WL 6788088, at *9 (E.D. La. Dec. 26, 2018) (quoting New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Found., v. Kirksey, 40 So. 3d 394, 407 (La. App. 4 Cir. 2010); Sea Tang Fisheries, Inc. v. You’ll See Sea Foods, 569 So. 2d 992, 995 (La. Ct. App. 1990)). Courts may disregard corporate separateness only when “fraud or deceit has been practiced by the shareholder acting through the corporation” or when shareholders disregard corporate formalities “to the extent that the corporation ceases to be distinguishable from its shareholders.” Riggins v. Dixie Shoring Co., 590 So. 2d 1164, 1168 (La. 1991). In Rodriguez, the Fifth Circuit emphasized that alter ego is not a mechanism for imposing strict products liability merely because entities share financial interests or ownership structure. 242 F.3d. at 577-78 (“There must be something more than mere unity of financial interest, ownership and control for a court to treat the subsidiary as the alter ego of the parent and make the 15

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 16 of 27 parent liable for the subsidiary’s tort.”). Rather, veil piercing is reserved for rare circumstances involving misuse of the corporate form to perpetrate fraud or injustice. Id. The court cautioned that alter ego is “an extraordinary remedy” and explained that corporate separateness is not disregarded simply because companies share common ownership, overlapping management, or financial interdependence. Id. Critically, the Fifth Circuit held that it was error even to charge the jury in a way that would have permitted them to treat affiliated defendants as manufacturers absent legally sufficient proof of veil-piercing factors and entered judgment for the defendant. Id. Thus, Plaintiff’s claims fail as matter of law because she improperly seeks to use conclusory alter ego allegations as a substitute for the required statutory element of manufacturing, yet offers no evidence of the fraud, injustice, or other exceptional circumstances necessary to pierce the corporate veil and impose liability upon either the non-manufacturing entities or the individuals. C. Plaintiff’s design defect claim fails as a matter of law. Plaintiff’s LPLA claims are fatally flawed. Plaintiff’s design defect theory, which posits that kratom is inherently too dangerous to be sold is fundamentally incompatible with the LPLA, which requires proof of a feasible alternative design. See La. R.S. § 9:2800.56(1). Furthermore, Plaintiff cannot establish the essential element of causation, a prerequisite for all LPLA claims. 1. Plaintiff’s claim fails for lack of a safer, feasible alternative design. a. Plaintiff alleges no alternative design is possible. Under the LPLA, a product is unreasonably dangerous in design only if, at the time it left the manufacturer’s control, “[t]here existed an alternative design for the product that was capable of preventing the claimant’s damage.” La. R.S. § 9:2800.56(1). Plaintiff has failed to produce any evidence identifying a specific, feasible alternative design for O.P.M.S. Silver that would have prevented Harmony’s death. Instead, Plaintiff’s own allegations concede that no such alternative 16

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 17 of 27 exists. By claiming it is “not scientifically possible” to make kratom safe, Plaintiff has judicially admitted her inability to satisfy a core element of her own claim. If no safe design is possible, then no alternative safer design is possible. This mandates summary judgment in Defendants’ favor. See Williams v. UPS, Inc., 2018 WL 1189687, at *3 (M.D. La. Mar. 7, 2018) (dismissing a design defect claim for failure to allege an alternative design); Sisk v. Sears, 959 F. Supp. 337, 339 (E.D. La. 1996) (dismissing design defect claim for lack of evidence that alternative design existed at time of accident). b. The lack of an alternative design triggers a cascade of legal failures. Even if Plaintiff could show the existence of an alternative design “capable of preventing the claimant’s damage” at the time the product left the manufacturer’s control, Plaintiff must also prove “[t]he likelihood that the product’s design would cause the claimant’s damage and the gravity of that damage outweighed the burden on the manufacturer of adopting such alternative design and the adverse effect, if any, of such alternative design on the utility of the product.” La. R.S. § 9:2800.56(2). Because Plaintiff has not and cannot identify any alternative design, Plaintiff necessarily cannot meet her burden to show either the “burden on the manufacturer of adopting any alternative design,” or “the adverse effect, if any, of such alternative design on the utility of the product.” These additional failures also mandate summary judgment. D. Plaintiff cannot establish causation, a necessary element of all LPLA claims. Plaintiff’s entire case collapses under the weight of a fundamental failure: the inability to prove causation. The LPLA requires a plaintiff to prove that a characteristic of the product proximately caused the claimant’s damage. La. R.S. § 9:2800.54(A). Plaintiff’s attempt to link O.P.M.S. Silver to her daughter’s death fails at every critical step of the causal analysis—from the 17

Plaintiff cannot show that OPMS Silver kratom was the cause of the harm. Before any analysis of toxicology or foreseeability, a plaintiff must first establish a basic factual link: that the decedent consumed the defendants’ product. Such an inference is not only pure speculation, but profoundly inequitable. “Testimony based on conjecture or speculation is insufficient to raise an issue of fact to defeat a summary judgment motion.” Ruiz v. Whirlpool, Inc., 12 F.3d 510, 513 (5th Cir. 1994) (plaintiffs could not meet their burden to show defendant was the supplier of the allegedly harmful product based solely on speculation). Plaintiff has not offered and cannot offer any evidence to create a triable issue of fact that a 150 ng/mL mitragynine level could have caused Ms. Moller’s fatal cardiac event thus providing yet another reason for summary judgment. 20

Co., 539 So. 2d 66, 70 (La. App. 2nd Cir. 1988) (finding defective tree “was not a legal cause of the accident because it was not reasonable for the owner of the tree to anticipate the falling of the limb would result in this kind of accident”). The central question is whether it was foreseeable to a manufacturer in February 2023 that a 150 ng/mL concentration of mitragynine could exacerbate a rare coronary anomaly and result in death. The undisputed evidence shows it was not. The scientific literature available in February 2023 did not identify a risk of death from such a low concentration of mitragynine. Defendants had no duty to warn of an unknown and unforeseeable risk. “To successfully maintain a failure-to-warn claim under the LPLA, a plaintiff must demonstrate that the product in question has a potentially damage-causing characteristic and that the manufacturer failed to use reasonable care to provide an adequate warning about this characteristic.” Stahl v. Novartis Pharmaceuticals Corp., 283 F. 3d 254, 264 (5th Cir. 2002). To meet the first prong of this test, a plaintiff must provide evidence about the “cause, frequency, severity, or consequences” of the dangerous characteristic in question or face summary dismissal. Grenier v. Medical Engineering Corp., 243 F. 3d 200, 205 (5th Cir. 2001) (dismissing plaintiff’s failure to warn claim for lack of evidence as to the “cause, frequency, severity, or consequences” of the alleged damage-causing characteristic left “the scope of [any] duty to warn unclear.”) Under the LPLA, a manufacturer has a duty to warn, but only if the manufacturer knew or should have known of the risk. The LPLA provides a complete defense where “at the time the product left his control, [the manufacturer] did not know and, in light of then-existing reasonably available scientific and technological knowledge, could not have known of the characteristic that caused the damage or the danger of such characteristic.” La. R.S. § 9:2800.59(B). This “state-of-the-art” defense is dispositive here. The specific risk that a low dose (or any dose) of mitragynine could fatally exacerbate death in someone with a rare coronary anomaly was not known or reasonably knowable to the scientific community in February 2023. The scientific literature did not identify such a danger. SOF ¶¶ 92, 95–103, 106. Defendants cannot be held liable for failing to warn of a risk that science had not identified (and still has not identified). 2. Plaintiff cannot show that any alleged failure to warn caused injury. 22

Ariens Company, 2025 WL 786035, at *6 (E.D. La. Mar. 12, 2025). “In addition to proving cause-in-fact, a plaintiff must also demonstrate that the inadequate warning was the most probable cause of his injury.” Scott, 2025 WL 786035, at *6 (citing Wheat v. Pfizer, Inc., 31 F.3d 340, 342 (5th Cir. 1994)). Plaintiff has not provided any evidence from which a reasonable jury could conclude an inadequate warning was the most probable cause of her injury, so summary judgment is warranted. a. The O.P.M.S. Silver product included an adequate warning that Plaintiff admits was effective. Under the LPLA, “[a] manufacturer is required to provide an adequate warning of any danger inherent in the normal use of its product which is not within the knowledge of or obvious to the ordinary user.” Hinson v. Techtronic Industries Outlets, 126 F. Supp. 3d 747, 758 (W.D. La. 2015). Stahl establishes a clear, two-part test for adequacy: the warning must both lead the ordinary user or handler to contemplate the danger in using the product … and to either use it safely … or decline to use it. Stahl v. Novartis Pharmaceuticals Corp., 283 F.3d 254, 271 (5th Cir. 2002) (emphasis added). The O.P.M.S. Silver label at issue here meets this standard precisely. It contained clear warnings that “[i]ngesting Mitragyna Speciosa can be dangerous,” and directed the user multiple times to seek professional medical advice before use.6 SOF ¶¶ 88, 89. Critically, Plaintiff’s own testimony concedes that the warning accomplished exactly what the law requires. First, Plaintiff’s confirmed she understood the danger of ingesting the product: “[The label] says it is unapproved for dietary ingredients . . . so you shouldn’t consume it.” SOF ¶ 89. This admission directly 6 The label instructs to “[c]onsult your healthcare professional to determine if this product is right for you, and if so, how to use it safely,” to “[c]onsult your physician about potential interactions, other possible complications, and precautionary measures before considering this product” and “[i]nform your physician of the alkaloid content, labeled on the package.” SOF ¶ 89. 23

See Stahl, 283 F.3d at 271 (requiring a warning that leads the ordinary user to “contemplate the danger in using the product”). The label led her to the exact conclusion that there was a danger associated with consumption—so much so that she concluded one “shouldn’t consume it.” Second, Plaintiff’s testimony confirms she understood the label guides users to make the choice to either use the product safely or not at all. When complaining that the label instructs users to consult a physician, Plaintiff conceded that this advice would lead to a clear, binary choice: “The only thing they’re going to tell you is don’t take or do take.” SOF ¶ 89 (emphasis added). This fatal admission satisfies the Stahl’s second prong. The very outcome Plaintiff describes— prompting a user to decide whether to “don’t take or do take” the product—is the exact legal function of an adequate warning. See Stahl, 283 F.3d at 271 (requiring a warning that leads a user “to either use it safely . . . or decline to use it”). Plaintiff’s admissions confirm that the O.P.M.S. Silver label accomplished both of its required legal functions: it warned her of danger, and it instructed her on how to make a safe choice. The warning was legally adequate as a matter of law, and her LPLA claim fails. b. Any further warning would have been futile. Even if a more specific warning were required (and it is not), proximate cause also cannot be shown because any further warning would have been futile. “Once a plaintiff proves that the lack of an adequate warning or instruction rendered the product unreasonably dangerous, his cause in fact burden is assisted by a presumption: when a manufacturer fails to give adequate warnings or instructions, a presumption arises that the user would have read and heeded such admonitions.” Bloxom v. Bloxom, 512 So. 2d 839, 850 (La. 1987). However, this presumption is rebutted by evidence that “an adequate warning or instruction would have been futile under the 24

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-1 Filed 03/02/26 Page 25 of 27 circumstances.” Id. (ruling as a matter of law that an adequate warning in the owner’s manual would be futile where plaintiff admitted “he had not read any part of his owner’s manual”). Iin Hinson, the court concluded that the presumption the plaintiff would have heeded a warning that a pressure washer could break was rebutted when “the defendants have presented evidence showing the plaintiff ignored other instructions and warnings contained within the Operator’s Manual that accompanied the pressure washer.” Hinson, 126 F. Supp. 3d at 758. Based on the evidence that the plaintiff ignored other instructions and warnings, the Court found “no reasonable basis to believe that even if the defendants had included a warning that the handle of the pressure washer might break, the plaintiff would have altered his actions” and so “defendants are entitled to summary dismissal of the plaintiff’s failure to warn claim.” Id. The same outcome is warranted here. The presumption that Harmony would have heeded an additional warning is rebutted by the undisputed fact that Harmony did not heed the existing warning. The label explicitly instructed the user to consult a physician before use. There is no evidence Harmony did. SOF ¶ 90. In fact, Plaintiff has repeatedly represented Harmony had not seen a physician since 2021. SOF ¶ 90. By disregarding the clear directive to seek medical advice, she broke the causal chain. Kratom (Mitragynia speciosa Korth) is a tree-like plant native to Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and other parts of southeast Asia. Indigenous users create a “juice” by boiling fresh kratom leaves for several hours that is then diluted with hot water to make kratom tea. Kratom is used in traditional environments to treat diarrhea, hypertension, cough, fever, impotence, and other ailments. Kratom is used by manual laborers for its mild stimulant effects, a replacement remedy for individuals with problematic opioid use, and as a mild analgesic agent. In the west, many different kratom formulations are available, including tinctures, extracts, capsules, softgels, concentrated products, as well as dried leaf powders and cut leaf material. 5

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-14 Filed 03/02/26 Page 7 of 66 Ava Conger, Esq. December 18, 2025 Page 6 Kratom in western countries is most commonly used as a remedy for opioid addiction, chronic pain, depression, and anxiety. 19. The neurobehavioral effects of kratom are more subtle than the commonly described stimulant effects at low doses and opioid effects at higher doses. Low doses of kratom increase alertness, energy, and talkativeness. At doses greater than 5 grams, however, kratom users describe the persistence of heightened alertness coupled with analgesia. These effects account for the use of kratom as a mild stimulant for manual laborers, a replacement remedy for individuals with problematic opioid use, and as a mild analgesic agent. 20. Some of the biological effects of kratom arise from binding of alkaloidal components to a number of neurotransmitter receptors in the central nervous system, including the µ-opioid (MOR), κ-opioid, serotonergic (5-HT), and alpha (α1) receptors, among others. MOR activity is particularly important. MOR activation mediates pain, respiratory rate, gastrointestinal transit time, nausea, and pruritis, among other effects. Each of these effects is mediated via distinct signaling pathways following binding of an agonist to the MOR receptor. 21. Classical opioid agonists (e.g., morphine and fentanyl) are “unbiased” agonists in that they indiscriminately activate all biological effects mediated by MOR. Kratom is different. The most prevalent—and best studied—alkaloid in kratom is mitragynine. In contrast to classical unbiased MOR agonists, mitragynine is a “biased” agonist in that it produces some, but not all, effects that arise from receptor binding of a classical MOR agonist such as morphine or fentanyl. 22. For example, while mitragynine produces analgesia, it does not produce the stupor characteristic of classic, unbiased MOR agonists. Instead, kratom produces increased alertness. Furthermore, mitragynine does not produce the respiratory depression that is a leading cause of mortality from classical unbiased MOR agonist overdose (Macko 1972; Varadi 2016; Kruegel 2019; Boyer 2012). 23. In fact, the clinical features as well as the time course of the toxidrome from kratom has never been described. Testing for mitragynine is generally limited to commercial forensic companies and medical examiner offices. Mitragynine itself undergoes postmortem redistribution; the postmortem concentration of mitragynine measured by forensic laboratories is over three times higher than premortem blood. 24. In general, adverse events attributed to kratom have been derived from database studies, poorly controlled case reports, or small case series, each of which has serious deficiencies in patient background information, including medical, social, or family history; clinical evaluation; scene findings; or analytical technique. The postmortem concentration of mitragynine identified in Ms. Moller’s blood was 158 ng/mL as measured by the Gerona lab (St. Tammany Parish Coroner records); commercial clinical laboratories measured the mitragynine concentration as 150 ng/mL (St. Tammany Parish Coroner records). Mitragynine undergoes postmortem redistribution, a process where the concentration of a substance changes following death. The available scientific literature demonstrates that the postmortem concentration of mitragynine is approximately triple that of pre- mortem measurements (Osawa 2025). To a reasonable degree of medical certainty, therefore, Ms. Moller’s premortem concentration of mitragynine was approximately 50 ng/mL, a value that occurred in human clinical trials involving kratom. Notably, none of the participants in these studies developed cardiac toxicity, much less a life-threatening event. Ms. Moller did not die from her kratom use. 76. In fact, medical examiners initially noted that the cause of death was “chronic liver congestion.” Chronic liver congestion is a medical condition often associated with right heart failure; backup of blood (i.e., “congestion”) into the liver produces fibrotic changes that become apparent even on visual inspection of the liver. Notably, kratom has not been associated with chronic liver congestion, even among patients where right heart failure was putatively associated with distant and undefined kratom ingestion (Alameh 2025). 77. Although I agree with the medical examiner’s finding that Ms. Moller died from complications of her unrecognized congenital heart disease—that has a recognized association with sudden cardiac death—I find that the medical examiner errs in failing to consider adequately the pharmacophysiology of the full range of substances identified on postmortem testing. 78. I find that the medical examiner errs in determining that Harmony Moller’s kratom use contributed to her death. In fact, the pharmacophysiology of kratom is more likely to be protective against cardiac sudden death in a patient such as Ms. Moller who had a high takeoff of the coronary artery with an acute angle of origin complicated by an inferior aortic flap. Following ingestion, mitragynine exerts parasympathetic effects on the cardiovascular system (Saengmolee 2022; Prevete 2024). These effects, measured generally as a slight decrease in systolic and diastolic blood pressure even in the setting of greater alertness, are insufficient to contribute to morbidity and mortality of an individual with high takeoff of the coronary artery with an acute angle of origin of the coronary artery complicated by an inferior aortic flap (Saengmolee 2022; Prevete 2024).1 79. Caffeine is an over-the-counter stimulant that increases pulse rate and intra-aortic blood pressure, but caffeine also limits the elasticity (i.e., how much the blood vessel can expand in response to increased blood pressure) of the aorta. New York (NY): Columbia University. 1987. Narrative Report Clinical innovation and research investigations have formed the twin pillars of my academic career. My clinical contributions, the most important of which have been published in high-impact general medical journals, have been adopted internationally by clinicians working in emergency medicine, medical toxicology, pediatrics, infectious diseases, psychiatry, addiction medicine, and behavioral science. My body of work has substantively improved the treatment of highly lethal poisonings, identified the economic benefit of antidotes, increased the safety of dietary 46

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-14 Filed 03/02/26 Page 64 of 66 supplements, prevented pediatric overdose, informed management of opioid overdose, and boosted adherence to medications for common, intractable, and expensive medical conditions. My research career, supported continuously by NIH since 2001 and informed by observations I make as a bedside clinician, has emphasized two main areas of investigation. In a series of studies from 2007, I have pioneered the use of signal processing and machine learning to identify, in real time and in natural environments, relapse to cocaine use, behavioral transitions to increased health risk, emerging population-wide drug use behaviors, and the opioid sparing effect of machine learning-tagged music. My second field of study involves advanced technologies in health. My studies related to mobile biosensors have provided vivid, indisputable evidence of medication ingestion, detected opioid use as well as the development of opioid tolerance, and apps that modulate pain and anxiety. Recognizing the innovativeness of my science and its impact on multiple scientific disciplines, NIH awarded me a K24 mid-career award—the first emergency physician to be so funded—so that I could mentor junior faculty into skilled clinician-scientists. This funding led to a flowering of my academic career as the scope of my research expanded even further. My research grown to include web semantic learning to identify new patterns of psychoactive substance use, Bluetooth- labeled naloxone syringes to determine the fate of opioid antidote distributed into the community, and ingestible biosensors that measure, rather than infer, the actual time at which patients take their medications, and the study of machine learning-tagged music as an intervention for pain and anxiety. One outgrowth of my mentoring efforts has been improvements in academic practice and the study of methods to accelerate academic productivity. My initial effort in this area emphasized writing retreats that focused on providing a linkage of junior authors to senior faculty; follow up work focused on establishing iterative writing periods where participating junior faculty provided critiques and writing suggestions for others’ work. By replacing a didactic approach to authorship with faster support and editorial review, this fundamental advance accelerated the academic careers of junior faculty, particularly those of female faculty. I have also extended my mentoring work to the study of resident wellness where I led a study evaluating commercial sound-cancelling sleepbuds to help clinicians transition to and recover from overnight shifts. The innovation of my work has been recognized by four different academic disciplines. First, I was named the 2008 NIH Distinguished Lecturer in Natural Products Neurosciences, an award from the medicinal chemistry community for my studies related to adverse effects of kratom. Then, in 2011, I received the American College of Medical Toxicology’s annual Research Award for career accomplishments in research investigations. In 2013, my work related to graphical presentations of complex clinical data was recognized by the engineering and mHealth communities with the Best User Experience Award at MIT Media Lab’s Health and Wellness Innovations 2013. My studies to extend the capacity of wearable biosensors into drug abuse treatment was applauded by the Society of Behavioral Medicine with the 2015 Citation Award. In 2016, I was the overall winner of the Medstro Innovations in Healthcare Challenge for my work related to digital pills for medication ingestion monitoring. Finally, in 2018 I was named a Fulbright Scholar to Malaysia to study the pharmacophysiology of kratom in Malaysian heroin injectors. Few emergency physicians have been recognized by such disparate academic disciplines, and I look forward to creating a pipeline of clinician scientists capable of making my own accomplishments look small. 47

I have no other testimonial history in the last five years. FACTUAL BASIS FOR OPINIONS Factual Background on Kratom 6. Kratom is legal in the United States and in most countries worldwide. The kratom tree from Southeast Asia is related to the coffee tree, with kratom leaf powder ingested traditionally as a tea to increase energy and improve mood, like coffee. Kratom users also self-report using kratom for analgesia and to help in managing their opioid or other drug use disorder and drug withdrawal (Henningfield 2023). Kratom contains multiple alkaloids, with the primary alkaloid being mitragynine, representing approximately 2% of the plant weight (Hassan 2013). 7. Basic research, epidemiological and surveillance kratom data, and recent clinical kratom research indicate that kratom has a diverse and complex pharmacology and is not an opioid based on its chemistry, structure, or pharmacology (Kruegel 2016). 3

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-32 Filed 03/02/26 Page 5 of 127 8. Scientific evidence indicates that kratom should not be scheduled. After a thorough review of the evidence, the Assistant Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (“DHHS”), Admiral Giroir, rescinded the Food and Drug Administration (“FDA”) request to schedule kratom, mitragynine, and 7-hydroxy-mitragynine (Giroir 2018). He refuted the claims of an imminent public health risk, refuted claims of mitragynine as cause of death in FDA-cited overdoses and stated that opioid overdoses and deaths would likely increase if kratom was scheduled. 9. In a recent independent review of kratom, mitragynine, and 7-hydroxy- mitragynine, the Expert Committee on Drug Dependence, as part of the United Nations Commission on Narcotic Drugs also determined that these substances should not be scheduled due to the lack of data supporting harm (United Nations Commission on Narcotic Drugs, 2021). 10. The scientific evidence on the abuse potential of kratom, mitragynine, and 7- hydroxy-mitragynine is like many other non-scheduled compounds (Henningfield 2022a). These authors updated the 8-factor analysis for kratom, finding that there was no evidence of an imminent risk to public health, and that a Schedule I listing (the only option for substances that are not FDA- approved for therapeutic use) could produce a public health risk by increasing drug overdoses by people using kratom to abstain from opioids. We concluded that public health was better served by assuring continued access to kratom products by consumers. Kratom alkaloids and derivatives are also in development as safer and/or more effective medicines for treating pain, substance use disorders, and mood disorders. Scheduling kratom would criminalize consumers, seriously impede research, and could increase drug overdose deaths. 11. When taken responsibly, kratom offers a harm reduction tool for opioid use disorder. Dr. Nora Volkow, Director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse, testified before the U.S. Congress in May 2022 on the importance of kratom as a harm reduction tool amid the opioid overdose epidemic. In addition, individuals self-report use of kratom to help manage their opioid or other drug use disorders (NIDA 2025). Individuals who frequently consume large doses of kratom can develop kratom dependence and experience withdrawal during abstinence; however, 4

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-32 Filed 03/02/26 Page 6 of 127 the withdrawal is considered much milder than opioid withdrawal and is generally self-managed (Henningfield 2022a). 12. Recent preclinical data showed no respiratory depression in rats that received doses much higher than equivalent human kratom doses. Drs. Henningfield, Rodricks, Magnuson and I conducted research on the high kratom doses (up to 400 mg/kg) orally administered to rats and compared its effects to those administered oxycodone, a potent opioid (Henningfield 2022b). Oxycodone administration produced significant dose-related respiratory depressant effects and pronounced sedation with one death each at 60 and 150 mg/kg. Mitragynine did not yield significant dose-related respiratory depressant or life-threatening effects, even at the highest doses. Sedative-like effects, milder than produced by oxycodone, were evident at the 400 mg/kg dose. Consistent with mitragynine’s pharmacology that includes partial μ-opioid receptor agonism with little recruitment of the respiratory depressant activating β-arrestin pathway, mitragynine produced no evidence of respiratory depression at equivalent doses many times higher than taken by humans. 13. Recent human controlled kratom administration data established the safety and lack of abuse liability of 4000 mg oral dried kratom leaf powder doses containing up to 53.2 mg mitragynine in the first large-scale randomized, placebo-controlled, escalating single and multiple 15-day oral kratom double blind administration study in 200 healthy normal participants (Huestis 2024a). Four thousand mg dried kratom leaf powder containing 6.65 to 53.2 mg mitragynine was administered as a single dose or as 15 consecutive daily doses. As the dose of mitragynine increased, the peak concentrations of mitragynine and its metabolite, 7-hydroxy-mitragynine, increased dose-proportionally. Following a single 53.2 mg mitragynine dose in 4000 mg dried kratom leaf powder, the mean mitragynine concentration in 12 healthy normal volunteers was 130 ng/mL (range 34.2-204 ng/mL). 14. There was extensive safety monitoring of the participants throughout the 47-day study that found no serious adverse events following active single or multiple dose dried kratom leaf powder or placebo (Huestis 2024b). Treatment emergent adverse events (TEAE) were recorded if a study participant’s pre-existing condition or state changed or worsened at any time 5

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-32 Filed 03/02/26 Page 7 of 127 during the study regardless of whether they received a placebo or test article, therefore, TEAE may or may not be related to the study intervention. TEAE generally increased as dose increased. Steady state mitragynine and 7-hydroxy-mitragynine concentrations were achieved within seven to nine days, and drug concentrations did not accumulate greater than two-fold after multiple dosing. Dizziness, nausea and feeling of relaxation were the most common TEAE following the single kratom leaf powder dose. For context, the dietary supplement melatonin can also potentially cause dizziness, nausea, and feelings of relaxation (Mayo Clinic melatonin 2025). After multiple kratom leaf powder doses, headache, feeling hot, increased alanine transaminase concentrations and nausea were the most common TEAE (Huestis 2023). Overall, oral kratom was well-tolerated without significant cardiovascular, neurological, or hepatic adverse events. There were no seizure events in any participant across the study. The TEAE that is most closely aligned with abuse potential is euphoric mood, or an exaggerated feeling of physical and emotional well-being and optimism. Although there were sporadic, single reports of euphoric mood, there was no dose- abuse liability relationship following single kratom doses. Following the highest multiple kratom dose, there were no reports of euphoric mood, suggesting low abuse potential at the investigated doses. This study provides new safety data in humans and shows a low abuse potential at kratom doses up to 4000 mg kratom leaf powder. 15. There are few reports of kratom poisonings and overdoses in which kratom is the sole cause or a contributing cause of injuries in the United States over the past ten years based on the 2022 National Poison Data System report (Gummin 2023). In 2022, 2,064,875 human drug exposures were reported, with analgesics representing 29.6% of drug-involved exposures. Kratom/mitragynine was not classified as an analgesic in this report. Of over two million human exposures, 2,622 resulted in death that was judged to be drug-exposure related. Of these 2,622 drug exposure deaths, mitragynine was listed in only one death report (0.04%): a 25-year-old female died of a propranolol overdose with a 2000 ng/mL highly toxic propranolol blood concentration. Mitragynine was listed as contributory with a 330 ng/mL blood concentration. 6

In 127 mitragynine impaired-driving cases in living individuals, mean and median blood mitragynine concentrations were 133 and 62 ng/mL (8.8–1000 ng/mL). Prior to these published NMS Labs data, many deaths with mitragynine concentrations far less than 1000 ng/mL listed mitragynine as the cause of death, leading many to overestimate the toxicity of kratom/mitragynine. The Papsun 2023 manuscript suggests that blood mitragynine concentrations alone up to 1000 ng/mL are unlikely to cause death. Marilyn A. Huestis retired as a tenured senior investigator and Chief, Chemistry and Drug Metabolism Section, IRP, National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health in 2016 after 23 years of conducting controlled drug administration studies. She was an Adjunct Professor, University of Maryland School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD from 1999-2017. Currently, she is a Senior Fellow at the Institute on Emerging Health Professions, Thomas Jefferson University, Philadelphia, PA, Adjunct Professor, University of New Mexico, College of Pharmacy, Honorary Professor, Barts & London School of Medicine & Dentistry, Queen Mary University of London, England on the Smart Approaches to Marijuana (SAM) Science Advisory Board, and President of Huestis & Smith Toxicology, LLC. Her research program focuses on the neurobiology and pharmacokinetics of cannabinoid agonists, kratom/mitragynine, oral fluid drug testing, and driving under the influence of drugs. She published 595 peer-reviewed manuscripts and book chapters and hundreds of invited lectures and abstracts were presented at national and international meetings. Professor Huestis has an AB in biochemistry from Mount Holyoke College, a MS in clinical chemistry from the University of New Mexico, and a PhD in toxicology from the University of Maryland. Professor Huestis received a Doctor Honoris Causa from the Faculty of Medicine, University of Helsinki in Finland. Other important awards include the 2025 Widmark Award from ICADTS, 2023 CMCR Pioneer in Medicinal Cannabis Research Award, 2023 Mechoulam Award from ICRS, 2021 AACC Outstanding Lifetime Achievement Award, 2021 NSC Distinguished Service to Safety Award, 2021 AAFS Alexander O.
